newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Kohl holds firm on EMU timetable, criteria.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kohl holds firm on EMU timetable, criteria.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Tuesday refused to budge in his insistence that European monetary union (EMU) should start on time in 1999 on the basis of a rigorous reading of the single currency's guiding Maastricht treaty.
"We want the euro to come punctually on January 1, 1999. But it is clear this must not be at the expense of monetary stability," he wrote in a newspaper article.

Writing on the 40th anniversary of the signing of the Treaty of Rome which created the forerunner to today's European Union, Kohl said currency union would boost growth and jobs and secure Europe's competitive position in the world.
But he said candidate states alone bore the responsibility for meeting the Maastricht convergence criteria: "The stability criteria of the Maastricht treaty are not open to discussion."

Germany's leaders have insisted on a tight interpretation of Maastricht to win over a sceptical public which regards the deutschemark as a talisman which guided the country's post-war economic miracle.

But doubts are mounting that Germany itself can this year meet the treaty's budget deficit target of three percent of GDP which Bonn insists must be strictly adhered to for the launch of the euro currency to take place.

Hampered by a weak economy, record post-war unemployment and slack tax revenues, Finance Minister Theo Waigel has said welfare cuts and even tax increases could be needed this year to get inside the deficit target.
In a separate interview with the Die Zeit weekly, Kohl's heir-apparent Wolfgang Schaeuble said that fulfilling the convergence criteria was "an absolute priority" for Germany.
Schaeuble, who is parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), also said he strongly opposed a delay to European monetary union (EMU).

"We must fulfil the criteria, so that we do not have to postpone the euro. It is doubtful whether Europe would get a second chance," Schaeuble said in an interview released ahead of publication on Wednesday.
"If we do not hold to the three percent limit on the budget deficit, even this strong government will not have enough power to push through the euro," he said.

Germany's insistence on a strict reading of Maastricht is widely seen as a way to exclude countries which do not have a long-term record of monetary stability and whose participation could undermine confidence in the strength of the euro.

Those countries include Italy, whose Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said in Rome on Tuesday it would be in Europe's interests to postpone the start of economic and monetary union but that he saw no chance of EU partners negotiating a delay.
"We are all in a straitjacket," he said. "If the treaty had provided for an extra year that would have been helpful."
But he added he thought it would be impossible to re-write Maastricht at this late stage and stressed that Italy was not looking to rock the boat.
Schaeuble said that if Germany gave up its tough position, the process of monetary union could slip out of control.

"If we suddenly abandon a strict interpretation, then we would no longer have control. For me there is barely a greater evil in economic, financial and social policy than not achieving the three percent target," he told Die Zeit.
"We have to achieve something of which we are convinced. We also know that it worries a majority (of Germans). We must not reinforce those fears by softening the criteria."
